prompt: Describe the dialectical method Aristotle uses in De Anima, specifically how he engages predecessor views while developing his own account of the soul.

result.content:
## 1. Aristotle, Rhetoric, Πάθη, and State-of-Mind

Aristotle's dialectical procedure in *De Anima* cannot be appreciated apart from the broader rhetorical and practical context within which his investigation of the soul unfolds; indeed, the very concept of πάθος—those affections of the soul that the rhetorician must understand if persuasion is to be effective—serves as a hinge between the rhetorical treatment of human dispositions and the ontological inquiry into what the soul fundamentally is. In the opening book of *De Anima*, Aristotle raises the question of whether the affections of the soul are common to the ensouled body or belong to the soul alone, thus situating πάθη at the intersection of physics and psychology (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 4). This question historicizes what Heidegger would later thematize as Befindlichkeit, or state-of-mind, insofar as the Greek inquiry into affective life already discloses the fundamental attunement of human being to its world; (Heidegger 2009, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. [PAGE NEEDED]), the attempt to grant rhetoric "the basic function of the genuine understanding of being-there itself" indicates precisely how deeply Aristotle's rhetorical analyses penetrate into the structure of human existence (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 107). The soul's οὐσία, Heidegger further clarifies, signifies not a fixed substance but rather "a mode of being," such that when the soul is called οὐσία it refers to "a distinctive mode of being, namely the being of" the living creature in its situated world (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, pp. 32–34). Accordingly, the dialectical engagement with predecessors in *De Anima* I is not merely a catalogue of opinions but an exercise in exhibiting how earlier thinkers grasped—or failed to grasp—the enmattered character of πάθη, thereby preparing the ground for Aristotle's own hylomorphic account. The connection between rhetoric and psychology thus proves structural rather than incidental, since understanding πάθος as an enmattered λόγος demands that one attend simultaneously to the bodily and rational dimensions of affective experience (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 107). Multiple Authors writing on Heidegger's appropriation of Aristotle's rhetorical project confirm that "mind is not at all pure" and that thinking is dependent upon imagination and bodily sensation, so that "imagination is the Boden of noein" (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, pp. 118–119). This impurity of νοῦς, far from being an embarrassment, becomes the methodological warrant for beginning with the πάθη as they are lived rather than as they are abstractly theorized. 

## 2. Aristotle, Time-Definition, and Temporality

The dialectical confrontation with predecessors in *De Anima* presupposes a particular understanding of temporality that Aristotle's definition of time—χρόνος as the number of motion with respect to the before and after—both enables and constrains. (Heidegger 2009, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. [PAGE NEEDED]) this Aristotelian time-definition itself presupposes a more originary temporality, one disclosed through the ecstatic structure of Dasein's existence; specifically, the innovations in Heidegger's theory represent "the very fundamental commitment in Heidegger's theory to a temporal manifold, rather than to a linear sequence of past, present, and future 'nows'" (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, pp. 124–125). Aristotle's procedure in *De Anima* enacts this temporal dimension implicitly, for the doxographical survey of Book I retrieves what predecessors have said—what has-been-thought—and holds it toward the τέλος of a completed account, thus exhibiting a temporal structure of retention and anticipation. When Aristotle notes that previous thinkers "seem to have confined themselves to the human soul" and raises the question "whether it is everywhere homogeneous or not; and if not homogeneous, whether its various forms are different specifically or generically," he is marking the limits of inherited opinion and projecting forward toward his own inquiry (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 4). Heidegger's analysis in *Being and Time* clarifies that "Being and Time cannot be clarified in terms of the 'now'" and that "the 'now' is a temporal phenomenon which belongs to time as within-time-ness: the 'now' 'in which' something arises, passes away, or is present-at-hand" (Heidegger, *Being and Time*, pp. 386–387). Thus Aristotle's own sequential presentation—first the opinions of predecessors, then the aporiai, then the positive account—is itself a temporal movement whose ordering discloses a priority of the τέλος over the ἀρχή, a structural feature that Heidegger renders explicit by reinterpreting chronos through the lens of ecstatic temporality. 

## 3. Heidegger identifies the "now" as the basic unit of within-time-ness, the temporal index through which entities are encountered as arising, passing away, or persisting; specifically, the ecstatic mode of the "Present" reveals itself when contrasted with authentic temporality, since the "waiting-towards" that characterizes inauthentic engagement with the present discloses how Dasein ordinarily understands its temporal situation (Heidegger, *Being and Time*, pp. 386–387). Aristotle's own dialectical procedure unfolds within this dimension of public time: each predecessor's view is taken up as something that has been said at a particular juncture in the tradition and is then subjected to critical scrutiny in the present of investigation. The question of the soul's homogeneity and partitioning—"which ought we to investigate first, the whole soul or its parts?"—is posed as a methodological question within the temporal horizon of inquiry, not as a timeless logical puzzle (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 4). The Aristotelian rhetorical initiatives, moreover, prepare for Heidegger's treatment insofar as rhetoric already discloses the temporal structure of persuasion—the speaker addresses an audience in a present shaped by past experience and oriented toward future action (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, pp. 124–125). 143–144). Aristotle's doxographical method already enacts a nascent historicity: each predecessor's view is preserved, examined, and overcome in a movement that is irreducibly temporal. ## 4. Εἶδος in Aristotle and the Contrast with Platonic Forms

Aristotle's dialectical method in *De Anima* reaches one of its most consequential moments in the treatment of εἶδος, for it is here that the contrast with Platonic forms becomes explicitly operative. Where Plato treats the Forms as self-subsistent entities separated from sensible particulars, Aristotle redefines εἶδος as the formal cause immanent in the composite substance; accordingly, Aristotle describes the soul as "the first actuality of a natural organic body," thereby insisting that form is not separable from the organized body it actualizes (Papachristou, *Three Kinds or Grades of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima*, pp. 1–3). Heidegger elucidates this transformation by observing that for Aristotle, the "appearing" anticipated in τέχνη "is what determines the being-there-completed in its being-there, characterizes it in its being-there-as-house"—that is, the εἶδος functions not as a transcendent paradigm but as the immanent look of the completed being (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, pp. 162–164). The consequences for the dialectical treatment of the soul are substantial: Aristotle can criticize predecessors who, like certain Platonists, treat the soul as a separately existing substance, because his own hylomorphic framework demands that the soul be the form of a living body rather than an inhabitant of it. Aristotle highlights this contrast when he raises the difficulty of why the soul, if it were simply a material element, would form an animal only in mixtures and not in pure elements such as air or fire (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, pp. 16–18). As Caston observes, "we are in a better position to analyze" Aristotle's arguments against his predecessors than to evaluate their historical accuracy, since "it is his arguments, in any case, which matter most for understanding his position" (Caston, *Why Aristotle Needs Imagination*, pp. 3–4). The productive tension between εἶδος as shared across instances and εἶδος as necessarily individuated within a particular ensouled body is never finally resolved, yet it is precisely this tension that animates Aristotle's dialectical engagement with the entire tradition preceding him.
